name: Oklahoma Voice
title: State Question 847 would cap Oklahomans’ property tax growth. At what cost?
text:
Voters mark their ballots in the Oklahoma County Election Board on June 11 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A state question on Oklahoma general election ballots could slow the growth of property taxes, but it has raised concerns about the financial impact on public services.
If State Question 847 passes on Nov. 3, the assessed value of a homestead or agricultural property could increase by no more than 1.75% per year, down from the current cap of 3%. The fair cash value of non-homestead properties could rise by a maximum of 4% annually rather than 5%.
The state question also would add similar caps ranging from 0.35% to 1.75% for Oklahomans age 65 or older who make too much income to qualify for the “senior freeze,” which locks recipients’ property taxes at the value of the time they apply.
The ballot measure wouldn’t cut Oklahomans’ property taxes, but it would limit the increased tax costs property owners could face over time, which supporters say would give needed relief as other expenses rise. 
Others say the state question would slowly drain millions of dollars from schools, CareerTech centers and other core services that depend on property tax revenue.
Although the ballot language states the exact fiscal impact is “unknown,” the Oklahoma Tax Commission projected local tax jurisdictions would lose $45.78 million in revenue the next fiscal year, if the state question passes.
When extending that over 10 years, local government entities could lose out on $457.8 million, the Oklahoma State School Boards Association estimated.
OSSBA executive director Shawn Hime acknowledged nobody likes to pay property taxes “until you start thinking about all the things that you receive and the core services that are offered based on those taxes.”
“We have to have the resources available for core services like emergency management, our roads and bridges, our police and fire,” Hime said. “All of those things cost money, along with resourcing our schools so that we can have high-quality teachers in the classroom with every student.”
Oklahoma State School Boards Association executive director Shawn Hime speaks at an Oklahoma City Board of Education meeting Feb. 29, 2024, at the Clara Luper Center for Educational Services. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Oklahoma CareerTech state director Brent Haken estimated vocational learning centers alone would lose about $90 million over the next 10 years. Budgets would begin to constrict as inflation rises, he said, ultimately costing career training programs that help Oklahoma meet workforce demands.
“We will start to first be stagnant in program offerings, and then over time reduce because the cost of doing business will continue to rise while our cost of collections is not rising,” Haken said. “So, 10 years from now, you would expect to see less students enrolled in CareerTech than we do today if that measure were to pass.”
Local government entities still will receive more revenue than they did the year before, just at a lower rate, said House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow. 
Oklahomans have been asking their state lawmakers for relief from rising costs, which prompted the state Legislature to put SQ 847 up for a public vote, said Hilbert, who co-wrote the ballot measure.
Homeowners have been struggling under increasing home insurance costs and “through the roof” interest rates while “their house is getting hit with that maximum increase of 3% per year” in taxed valuation, he said.
“When you look at the national market of housing and interest rates, as a state government how much could we as a state do?” Hilbert said. “I’m not sure, but the one piece of that equation that we can certainly have an impact on is the property tax.”
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, left, debates a bill in the House chamber of the state Capitol in Oklahoma City on April 13. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Hilbert pointed to the expected $45.78 million decrease in property tax growth as an endorsement of the state question, not a drawback.
“At the end of the day, that’s $45 million that’s being saved to taxpayers, which I think is a good thing,” he said. “And so, I think that’s the crux of this argument, is the tax consumers who are against this bill are upset because they’re not going to be able to raise taxes by $45 million next year.”
The Oklahoma Farm Bureau, an organization representing farmers and ranchers, also has supported the state question. 
Agricultural properties sometimes lose money because of factors like drought, input costs, and fluctuating crop and livestock prices. Meanwhile, “property taxes on that land continue to steadily climb,” the Farm Bureau wrote in its voter guide. 
In Guthrie Public Schools, Superintendent Mike Simpson estimated property tax revenue generates about 30% of his district’s budget.
Bond issues, which also are paid through property tax collections, have been crucial in financing the construction of new school buildings, the cost of which has risen dramatically, Simpson said.
Guthrie Public Schools Superintendent Mike Simpson, right, attends an event in Edmond on Aug. 3. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Districts still paying back bond debt suddenly would have less revenue growth than expected, which Simpson said could cause a short-term increase in property tax millage rates. Hilbert said lawmakers considered this issue and adjusted the state question to mitigate it.
SQ 847 would limit districts’ long-term bonding capacity, Simpson said, and it would pinch school facility budgets that rely on property tax revenue.
“The relief (for taxpayers) will not be immediate at all,” he said. “It will be over time, and the net effect on the homeowner will be less advantageous to them than it will be a tremendous problem financially and a burden to the school districts and the entities that receive the property tax.”

name: WyoFile
title: Once they’re gone, they’re gone forever
text:
Does anyone remember when Wyomingites spoke with one voice and our representatives in Washington said, “Screw you”? I do.

Opinion

Remember The One Big Beautiful Bill? It was designed to reward the rich and add to our massive deficit. It did both quite well. It was also designed to sell off our public lands, an idea that more than 90% of Wyomingites surveyed opposed. Lawmakers from Montana said, “hell no,” and threatened to vote against the bill. So, the sponsors of the bill took Montana’s public lands off the auction block. 
What did our three courageous representatives in Washington do? They voted for it, without even a squeak. Fortunately technical factors removed that part of the bill, but U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman has doubled down by leading the charge to get rid of our public lands and roadless areas in spite of massive public opposition from her constituents. And now she is on her way to becoming our U.S. senator, where she would continue her war against public lands and Wyoming sportsmen and sportswomen. Sen. John Barrasso will continue to sell us down the river in his own quiet way. If elected, U.S. Congress hopeful Chuck Gray will do whatever he is told by the Trump administration; what that will be remains to be seen. Our “true conservative” state legislators, like Sen. Bob Ide, are no better; they want all federal public lands gone. 
Do not be fooled by the argument that Wyoming should manage what are now Bureau of Land Management lands, national forests, parks and monuments. While the feds manage lands for many uses, including beauty and recreation, Wyoming manages state-owned lands through the five-person Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners following one constitutionally mandated goal: to maximize income from the property over which it has jurisdiction. Just look at what the board did when it granted Prism Logistics a gravel mine lease on the face of Casper Mountain. Those beautiful state lands are used by citizens for hiking and general enjoyment. While the Natrona County community banded against the mine, the board leased it without considering the community’s desires. (The board later flipped its stance in the face of major public opposition to the project.) With that vote, they tried to gift the community an eyesore that we can enjoy every new day for eternity. The issue is on appeal before the Wyoming Supreme Court. Fingers crossed. 
The state of Wyoming lacks the resources of the federal government to manage the vast properties it would acquire if the proponents of the transfer were to succeed. The only solution would be to turn the land into money and divest ownership. Prime recreational land would be sold to the highest bidder so that some wealthy landowner would be able to fence and sign it off from us ordinary people. The rich would rejoice, as would the powerful mineral extractors, who would no longer suffer under the yoke of federal regulations. Of course, the less-appealing properties would remain in state hands, unless and until the land board could turn a nickel with them.
One need only look at the occasions when wealthy out-of–state “ranchers” from California or Texas have traded lands they have purchased to the land board for school sections of lesser financial value, with the exclusive goal of blocking public access to national forests or other public lands. If Wyoming gains federal properties, they will sell them off or exploit them — especially the desirable ones —  to our detriment. Imagine, “Mr. Musk, may I hunt on your so-called ranch?” I have fished in Colorado, where most of the land is privately owned. One either pays for the “privilege” or stands elbow to elbow with other fishermen on the few public pieces of water. We are so spoiled in Wyoming, we don’t even appreciate what we have. There is a reason out-of-staters come to Wyoming to fish and hunt.
Everyone should take the time to read the opinion from the U.S. 10th Circuit Court authorizing corner crossing to access BLM land. The decision turns on the federal Unlawful Enclosures Act. If the state of Wyoming succeeds in acquiring that land, the act would no longer protect us and corner crossing will become illegal trespass: a crime, and a gift to the landed few. 
Of course, it is not even clear that our national representatives want to put the public lands into state hands. My belief is that Rep. Hageman wishes to sell them off at the federal level, “to balance the budget.” Bull. That wouldn’t be a drop in the bucket, but once those lands are gone, they are gone forever. I am not an unmitigated fan of the feds, but on this issue I trust them more than the other side.
Is this really part of the Trump agenda?  Why do our representatives disregard what us Wyomingites think? Who is their master? Only one explanation makes sense: money. Where do mystery out-of-state campaign dollars come from? Could it be from persons who have plans for our public lands?
Cowboy ethics: “Ride for the brand.” Our delegation is truly “riding for the brand,” just not our brand. Let’s cure that problem when we vote.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Doug Jones tells Montgomery town hall he wants to ‘phase out the CHOOSE Act’
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones talked about his education policy plan and other topics during a town hall in Montgomery on Oct. 13, 2026. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones Tuesday fielded questions about education and other topics at a town hall in Montgomery
Speaking to a crowd of at least 100 people, Jones talked about giving teachers and retirees a cost of living adjustment and said he wanted to “phase out the CHOOSE Act,” the state’s effective school voucher program. Income caps on eligibility for the program will end on Jan. 1.
“It’s (the CHOOSE Act) going to ultimately, if it doesn’t kill public schools, it’s going to just cripple and such that we do the public, and then we are seeing that in the numbers of kids that are in public schools this year,” Jones said. “The first year of the CHOOSE Act, 5,000 to 6,000 folks dropped fewer kids. The next year it was 12,000. Why do you think it’s going to be next year when the income caps are gone and we start giving handouts to people who make a lot of money?”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Alabama State Schools Superintendent Eric Mackey said during the Alabama State Board of Education meeting last week that preliminary numbers showed 12,000 students were unenrolled from public schools. Mackey said while CHOOSE Act recipients made up some of the loss, the large drop in enrollment can’t be attributed to the voucher program alone.
Jones’ plan to phase out the program differs slightly from his earlier talks of ending school vouchers in the state entirely. Jones said he “started out candidly talking about eliminating it,” but because there are students already taking advantage of the program, he wants to phase out school vouchers instead.
“Those kids made a decision and their parents to change schools and benefited,” he said. “They believe so, and the income caps were on, so we’ll phase it out. But we’ll let those kids graduate.”
Jones also said he was “committed to making sure teacher raises go up,” but that his focus will be split with ensuring that educators have access to healthcare.
“Healthcare delivery in this state is a challenge. It’s really in a crisis right now because of the cost of health insurance, the fact that we didn’t expand Medicaid, and it is really crippling,” Jones said.
The Public Education Employee Health Insurance Plan (PEEHIP) board plans to ask the Legislature for a $222 million increase in the fiscal year 2028 budget due to rising health care costs.
One public school teacher asked what Jones thought about the Ten Commandments being displayed in schools because of how it could impact non-Christian students. Gov. Kay Ivey this spring signed SB 99, sponsored by Sen. Keith Kelley, which requires local school boards to display a poster of the Ten Commandments in fifth through 12th-grade classes and within common areas, in April. The bill went into effect on Oct. 1.
“I think we’ve got to have an attitude in this state that is more open and honest about who our neighbors are and where they are and what they are and have that respect. The Bible that I grew up with, the Sunday school lessons I grew up with, taught Christianity, but they also taught respect for others,” Jones said.
A kindergarten teacher asked if Jones would be willing to split money in the Education Trust Fund for turnaround schools, an initiative to help struggling schools in the state, to provide for all schools in the state and bring back teacher’s aides if elected.
Jones said the RAISE Act, which aims to create a needs-based funding model for K-12 schools, is on the right path to ensuring schools remain funded.
“There’s school systems that have foundations that help them because their residents will contribute to those foundations, and I don’t think they should be denied state funding. I’m not saying that, but there are, and I think the RAISE Act is a real good start of identifying those schools and putting extra money there,” he said.
Jones also addressed questions about data centers, repeating his call for a moratorium on new data center construction to give time to develop plans for the facilities. 
“I believe that a moratorium would probably not even last a year. I think if right now the governor, the Legislature, whoever said we’re not going to build these things until we get it all together, I think people are going to come to the table, and they’re going to see what we need to do,” Jones said.
Jones used Lowndes County, which approved plans for a hyperscale data center Tuesday despite community members disapproval, as an example of why a moratorium is needed. 
The data center in Lowndes County, called Project Red Clay, is a 800-acre facility that would be placed near a residential area.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: In swift reversal, Minneapolis Public Schools superintendant cancels plan to close schools
text:
Lyndale Elementary Schools students board the bus after school on Thursday, Jan. 9, 2025, in Minneapolis, Minn. (Photo by Ellen Schmidt/Minnesota Reformer)Minneapolis Public Schools Superintendent Lisa Sayles-Adams said she would no longer recommend closing any schools next school year, less than a month after first proposing closures. Board chair Collin Beachy said that he would not allow any resolutions to close schools for the 2027-28 school year to be placed on the board agenda this year. 
The state’s third largest school district runs 59 school buildings for approximately 29,000 students. The district recently analyzed buildings and determined more than half are considered “under-utilized,” or 70% of capacity or less. The district operates its buildings with significantly fewer students per building than other large Minnesota districts.
The announcement surprised some board members, including Director Sharon El-Amin, who said she was “blindsided” by the superintendent’s announcement at the beginning of the meeting. 
After seven community meetings over the prior two weeks, Sayles-Adams said the community made clear the district should not close schools. Sayles-Adams said this will mean the district will continue to spread its limited resources across schools in ways that do not provide equitable access to opportunities for all students. 
The district has not named specific inequities, but in recent years, parents have reported elementary students without access to music or art specialists, and middle and high school students who do not have access to world languages, music or art electives. The district’s high schools also have varying access to advanced coursework. 
By closing schools and concentrating resources in fewer buildings, the district’s plans would have guaranteed all students access to music, art and physical education in elementary schools, and diverse electives in middle and high schools, according to Sayles-Adams. The plan would have also provided all schools with academic interventionists to support students who are not meeting grade-level standards. Currently, academic interventionists are only available at schools with the federal low-income designation of Title I. 
The district is dealing with long-term fiscal issues related to declining enrollment — state aid is dependent on enrollment — and rising labor costs.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Advocates again ask South Dakota governor to endorse summer food program operating in 39 states
text:
A U.S. Department of Agriculture webpage explains the Summer Electronic Benefits Transfer program, which provides grocery benefits for families with eligible school-age children. (Photo by South Dakota Searchlight)Thirty-four South Dakota organizations and businesses have asked Gov. Larry Rhoden to support a program that offers debit cards for food to low-income families during the summer months.
The program is federally funded, but is administered by states. 
The governor’s deputy secretary of education told South Dakota Searchlight that the administration is “taking another look at the program requirements and associated costs” after years of resistance to accepting the federal money. The costs to set up the program and run it each summer “remain a significant consideration,” Deputy Secretary Laura Scheibe said in a written statement. 
The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Summer Electronic Benefits Transfer program offers $120 per child, at $40 per month across three months, to help eligible families buy groceries during June, July and August. The money can’t be used for prepared food.
South Dakota would be in line for $6.8 million, according to the nonprofit Food Research and Action Center, enough to cover 57,000 kids.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Families could get the per-child stipend if they’re enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, if they qualify for free or reduced price school lunches, or are enrolled in Medicaid, the federal health insurance program for people who have low incomes. The money would also be available for families who participate in the Food Distribution on Indian Reservations program, as well as for the families of kids without homes and those living in foster homes.
South Dakota is one of 11 states not offering the program this year The other non-participating states are Alaska, Florida, Idaho, Indiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Utah, all of which, like South Dakota, have Republican governors.
Iowa had previously opted out, but opted in for summer 2026. Wyoming also took part this year, so every state bordering South Dakota now participates. Tennessee lawmakers voted to fund the program this spring, but families there won’t be able to access it until next summer. 
To participate for the summer of 2027, South Dakota would need to signal its intention to do so by Jan. 1. 
Groups call on Rhoden to participate
Bread for the World South Dakota is the local chapter of a Washington, D.C.-based Christian nonprofit organization. 
The group sent a letter to Rhoden’s office last week asking him to participate in summer EBT next year. Among the 33 other signatories are the Salvation Army of Mitchell, the South Dakota Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, South Dakota Kids Count, the League of Women Voters South Dakota and the South Dakota Advocacy Network for Women.
Support from governor means state will cover gap in reduced-price school meals

The letter urges Rhoden “to help ensure that every child in South Dakota has consistent access to the nutrition they need to grow, learn, and thrive” during the summer months through summer EBT.
Bread for the World sent a similar letter to former Gov. Kristi Noem in 2023, urging participation for 2024. 
A handful of people and organizations reached out to Rhoden about the issue last year, Bread for the World’s Cathy Brechtelsbauer said, but the group wanted a more concerted effort this year, “because it’s ridiculous that we still don’t have it,” Brechtelsbauer said. 
“Everybody in South Dakota is paying for it through our federal taxes,” Brechtelsbauer said. “Kids are hungry here, too.”
Federal money pays for on-site meals across South Dakota during the summer, but Brechtelsbauer said those meals feed only 1 in 7 kids who’d be eligible for summer EBT payments.
“Not everyone is able to get to school in the summer,” she said. 
The EBT cards onto which the summer benefit payments are transferred can be used at grocers. Franklin Food Market of Sioux Falls and Team Buche Cares, the nonprofit arm of the Buche Foods chain of grocery and convenience stores, each signed the summer EBT letter of support.
State: Setup cost could be great
Earlier this year, Rhoden signed a bill into law covering the family portion of the price for reduced price school meals. His signature on the bill came after previous attempts to pass similar bills failed in earlier legislative sessions. 
The federal government pays half of ongoing administrative costs for summer EBT, but Scheibe, Rhoden’s deputy education secretary, said the estimated setup cost in 2024 was between $500,000 and $700,000.
“IT programming and additional staffing would be required,” she said in a Monday email.
The state House of Representatives Education Committee endorsed a bill in 2024 that would have put $150,000 a year toward paying the state’s share of program administration for summer EBT. The Legislature’s budget committee voted the bill down.
Dan Ahlers, the Democrat running against Rhoden for governor in the Nov. 3 general election, said support for summer EBT would be a given if he were elected.
“Honestly, that’s not even a question,” said Ahlers, who supports state-funded school lunches for all South Dakota public school students. “Of course I’d support that.”
The setup and administrative costs associated with the program would be “negligible” compared to the benefit for hungry kids, Ahlers said. 
“Even if it’s $150,000” a year to run the program, he said, “that’s nothing.”

text:
Members of the Alabama State Board of Education pose for a picture after its meeting on Oct. 8, 2026. Board members Thursday voted to approve a $6.8 billion budget request for fiscal year 2028.(Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama State Board of Education Thursday approved a $6.8 billion budget request for fiscal year 2028, a 4% increase over the current year.
The request, which must be approved by the Alabama Legislature, includes increases for Struggling Readers Beyond Grade 3, school breakfast and transportation.
The Alabama State Department of Education last year requested $6.59 billion and received $6.58 billion in the FY27 Education Trust Fund Budget, the current budget. The FY28 budget will go into effect on Oct. 1 of next year.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We want to make sure that every student, every adolescent is also a good reader, and that when they’re leaving third grade on grade level, they’re staying on or above grade level in fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth too,” said Alabama State School Superintendent Eric Mackey during the meeting. “So when they get in high school, they’re above grade level going into those high school courses.”
The request is the largest component of the ETF, which funds public K-12 and postsecondary education in the state. The ETF this year is budgeted at $10.4 billion.
The department wasn’t given any money for Struggling Readers Beyond Grade 3, a program to increase literacy for students after third grade, in the FY27 ETF. Officials are seeking $45 million for the program from the budget.
The board also requested a $56.1 million increase (9%) for the transportation program for local education agencies and a $2.4 million increase (20%) was requested for parental leave. Mackey said during last month’s board meeting the increase was to help with the rising costs bus drivers face such as rising diesel prices.
The department wants to maintain funding in other programs. 
The department is asking for $58 million for the RAISE Act, which aims to create a needs-based funding model for K-12 schools. The appropriation would be the same as FY27. The RAISE Act aims to get additional money to populations such as rural students, students in poverty and English Language Learners. 
The request will come in a year where funding is expected to be tight due in part to health insurance pressures and uncertainty and tax revenues. Mackey said he doesn’t anticipate getting the full amount funded.
“We’ll obviously work with the new governor, incoming governor’s office, and legislature about what that number looks like in the end,” Mackey said. “The request is close to $50 million. I doubt we’ll get all of it, but I do think we’re making a good case for why that needs to continue to grow.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Scholarship tax credit vouchers, a wolf in sheep’s clothing
description: I have seen firsthand the disparity in resources among school districts in Fairfield County. This tax credit codifies and deepens those inequities.
text:
For months, governors across the country have awaited U.S. Treasury guidelines on the use of a Federal Scholarship Tax Credit set to launch January 1, 2027. Those guidelines have now been released, and the picture they paint for public education is worse than we could have imagined.  
The FSTC would release tens of billions of federal dollars to scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs) to provide services ranging from special education and autism support to private school tuition and high-dosage tutoring for students. Taxpayers who donate to SGOs would receive a dollar-for-dollar credit up to $1,700 per individual, or $3,400 per household, with no income limits.  

Joslyn DeLancey

The Trump administration has said that federal tax credit funds would not be limited to private schools; public school students could, ostensibly, benefit. The Treasury’s newly released guidelines tell a different story. 
SGOs act as middlemen for private equity firms, and the FSTC’s launch will provide these brokers with a strong, steady, reliable cash flow. The guidance around the FSTC tax scheme not only lets SGOs keep a 10 percent cut of every contribution, but it also gives them full decision-making power over where that money goes. They could decide every dollar they receive, for example, goes to religious schools.  
Under those same guidelines, states cannot impose a single guardrail on these funds. They cannot earmark them for students from low-income families or ensure they don’t discriminate. They cannot ensure these funds go where they would do the most good. 
The newly released guidelines only underscore widespread concerns about tens of billions of taxpayer dollars pouring into private schools and private-equity-owned education service providers. Education decisions would no longer be in the hands of public school parents, teachers, and boards of education; they would transfer to wealthy financial and tech investors.  
On the face of it, a $1,700 tax credit, especially one that’s reported to help all students,  seems hard to argue against. Look at the fine print, though, and you’ll see that it’s another voucher scheme designed to almost exclusively benefit the wealthy, direct money to private schools and service providers, and leave students and families with the greatest need behind.  
As a Stamford resident, longtime public school teacher in Darien, and vice president of the Connecticut Education Association, which represents educators all over the state — including Bridgeport and Danbury— I have seen firsthand the disparity in resources among school districts in Fairfield County. This tax credit codifies and deepens those inequities.  
Under this new initiative, high income families in Fairfield County will have the luxury of choosing to divert their tax dollars to private educational programs. These programs don’t have to follow the same rules, and taxpayers will have little to no say over what happens with those scholarships. There’s no guarantee of equitable distribution, and one thing is for certain: those dollars will not find their way to our public schools.  
Governors have until December 31 to opt into this voucher scheme, and those who care about preserving and improving the quality of their state’s education system will take a hard pass.  
We don’t need a crystal ball to know how this private equity scheme will play out in Connecticut’s public schools.  We’ve had a front-row seat to private equity’s destruction and abandonment of local hospitals and nursing homes, saddling them with enormous debt, stripping services down to the bare minimum, cutting core staff and resources, then cashing out and leaving.  
This has already happened with private equity-owned education service providers as well, including FEV tutoring, which closed overnight, leaving families across 30 states scrambling.  
For those who are undecided about the tax credit, the following questions are helpful:  

How do we ensure smaller class sizes, equitable funding, and accountability in our public schools under this initiative?  
Public schools are already underfunded by the federal government, especially special education. If tax dollars are diverted to public programs, won’t we pay for the tax credit either in property or state taxes to make up the difference? 
This program will create winners out of a few private companies selling educational services. Wouldn’t that raise the cost for services delivered to public schools? 
Fairfield County has some of the best public-school systems in the state, and we pride ourselves on that. Do we want to risk the quality of our public schools?  

Tax credits and scholarships may sound really exciting. In this case, you’re not saving money, and you’re not necessarily helping kids in need. You’re just playing a shell game: moving public dollars into private systems. Connecticut could and should do better. Imagine if we truly committed to investing in our public schools instead of buying into gimmicks.  
If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.  
Say no to the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit.  
Joslyn DeLancey is vice president of the Connecticut Education Association.

name: VTDigger
title: Our schools are being crushed by state mandates
description:
A sharp drop in the state’s excess spending threshold is forcing Hartford to make deep cuts, even as expenses rise.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Our schools are being crushed by state mandates.
text:
This commentary is by Caty Sutton, the superintendent of the Hartford School District; the Hartford School Board; the Hartford School District leadership and the Hartford Education Association leadership.
It is with great disappointment, discouragement and disillusionment that we write to express our profound concerns about what transpired throughout the last legislative session. As we anticipate what will come this year, those decisions will significantly affect and shape our fate as a district.
First, the passage of Act 169 at the end of the last legislative session and the reduction of the excess spending threshold from 118% to 115.5% in one fiscal year are devastating to our district and local community. Our district now faces an almost $5 million reduction in our budget while continuing to absorb the catastrophic, ongoing impact of crushing healthcare insurance costs and crippling inflation.
To put the above into perspective, we are looking at potentially having to reduce our administration, professional staff and support staff by 25% — one in four of our workforce — to present a budget to our community below the excess spending threshold so we can avoid the penalty that the state would impose.
At the same time, we continue to face the Vermont Agency of Education‘s ongoing accountability efforts, requiring districts to engage in significant and unfunded, unsupported initiatives. So, eviscerate our budgets, but expect our staff to take on even more?
All of this comes as the Legislature continues PCB testing in schools while leaving districts already affected in limbo, with little or no funding for mandated quarterly testing and no resources for remediation or abatement. These costs could amount to millions of dollars, leaving local taxpayers to fund a state-mandated response to a serious safety hazard.
We are also being given almost no lead time or transition period to adopt a new Medicaid reimbursement model, which will change how we are reimbursed and involve an entirely new system, requiring hours of training and implementation for staff who must deliver and adopt this approach.

READ MORE

Finally, let’s not forget that Act 170 places us in a Cooperative Educational Service Area (CESA) by statute. Since we were incorrectly placed by the Legislature in the Northeast region, we must also undergo an arduous process laid out in the statute to move from the Northeast into the Vermont Learning Collaborative, with which we have already been collaborating for two years, while simultaneously engaging in district merger committee conversations with regional neighbors who are in a different CESA region and facing the same challenging budget reductions. 
It is beyond challenging to believe that there is not a concerted effort to discredit, disenfranchise and essentially gut public education in Vermont, beginning with this fiscal year and the impossibility of our current budgeting circumstances.
Our community does not deserve this. Our educators have dedicated their careers and their lives to serving our students with integrity and care, and now we are put into the position of radically overhauling our district. For what, exactly? Neither the agency, the Legislature nor the governor has supplied us with any semblance of a realized vision for what this education transformation will give our students as a result of these profoundly damaging changes, and none of these entities has supplied us with the data and evidence that this transformation will lead to cost savings for our taxpayers. 
Our community did not ask for district merger studies, PCBs, changes to Medicaid and additional requirements from the agency. We just want to continue to do what we do best: provide the best possible education and support to our students with the funding our community is willing and able to provide.
Going forward, we expect our local delegation to revisit the abrupt and crushing impact that this reduction to the excess spending threshold will have on our district and to advocate for changes to slow down this process. We also expect them to push for allocation of funding to continue to ensure the law is followed and we do not incur the infinite costs of PCB testing, remediation and abatement. And we expect them to scrutinize the unrealistic timelines and processes related to the formation of CESAs and the district merger committee study groups.
In short, we expect our local delegation to take care of our community, which is struggling to breathe under the weight of the myriad costs of imposed mandates.
Please help us to save our most valuable community resource and advocate for a future with a strong public education system. Center our students, and consider who among us is the most vulnerable and requires the most support. Remember that public education is a fundamental and most vibrant component of Vermont democracy and community life. 
Please give us a lifeline to survive.
